question: What is the main job of our respiratory system?

options.B: Bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
options.D: Filtering bacteria out of the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! The lungs trade gases with every breath we take—bringing in fresh oxygen our body loves and blowing out waste carbon dioxide. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do lung problems often affect the rest of the body?

options.A: Lung infections spread directly to the brain within hours
options.B: Every organ relies heavily on a steady supply of oxygen from the lungs
options.C: Poor breathing causes the stomach to stop digesting food completely
options.D: The heart stops pumping blood when the lungs become inflamed

explanation: You got it! If the lungs aren't working well, oxygen delivery drops, and every single tissue in the body starts to suffer. Oxygen is food for our cells! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h1)

question: What do we call a dangerously low level of oxygen in the blood?
explanation: Well done! 'Hypo-' means low, and 'oxemia' refers to oxygen in the blood. Put them together and you have hypoxemia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which type of breathing problem involves a dangerous buildup of carbon dioxide?

options.A: A buildup of carbon dioxide due to poor ventilation
options.B: A sudden drop in oxygen caused by fluid in the alveoli
options.C: High blood pressure inside the arteries of the lungs
options.D: A complete collapse of the lung tissue from air in the chest

explanation: Correct! When a patient isn't moving air in and out well enough (poor ventilation), carbon dioxide gets trapped inside. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h2)

question: What actually is 'cor pulmonale'?

options.A: Bleeding into the chest cavity following trauma
options.B: An infection of the lining surrounding the lungs
options.C: Right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease
options.D: A sudden collapse of a lung lobe due to a blocked airway

explanation: You nailed it. Long-term lung trouble makes the heart work extra hard on the right side, eventually leading to right-sided heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h3)

question: A patient develops cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease. What sign might you spot as a nurse?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood glucose levels
options.B: Sudden sharp chest pain and absent breath sounds
options.C: Bright red blood coming up when coughing
options.D: Swollen lower legs and distended neck veins

explanation: Spot on! Since the right side of the heart is struggling to pump forward, fluid backs up into the body, causing swollen legs and puffy neck veins. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h3)

question: In simple terms, what is atelectasis?

options.A: An abnormal collection of air in the pleural cavity
options.B: A severe bacterial infection inside the lung tissue
options.C: The collapse or closure of a lung resulting in reduced gas exchange
options.D: High pressure inside the blood vessels of the lungs

explanation: Correct! Atelectasis happens when tiny air sacs (alveoli) deflate or collapse, making it harder to trade gases. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h4)

question: How does fluid in the chest cavity (pleural effusion) make it hard to breathe?

options.A: Fluid enters the alveoli and destroys the natural surfactant
options.B: It blocks the main windpipe and chugs off air supply
options.C: Fluid physically presses against the lung, stopping it from expanding fully
options.D: It forces the heart to beat too fast, causing sudden shock

explanation: You got it! The fluid takes up space in the chest and squeezes the lung from the outside, so it can't puff up nicely when breathing in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h4)

question: What fills the chest space when a patient has a hemothorax?
explanation: Easy and clear! 'Hemo' means blood, and 'thorax' means chest. It's blood inside the chest cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why is a tension pneumothorax such a major emergency?

options.A: Trapped air builds up pressure and shifts the heart and major blood vessels
options.B: It stops the kidneys from producing urine within minutes
options.C: It floods both lungs with thick, yellow mucus
options.D: It causes an immediate massive infection in the bronchial tubes

explanation: Correct! Trapped air keeps stacking up like a balloon, pushing everything in the chest sideways and stopping blood from returning to the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h5)

question: If a patient holds onto too much carbon dioxide because they aren't breathing deeply enough, what acid-base imbalance happens?
explanation: Well done! Carbon dioxide acts like an acid in the body. If it builds up in the lungs, the blood becomes too acidic—hence respiratory acidosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h6)

question: A patient is having a panic attack and breathing way too fast. What are they at risk for?
explanation: Spot on! Breathing too fast blows off too much carbon dioxide. Losing too much acid makes the blood basic (alkaline), causing respiratory alkalosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is usually the very first clue that a patient's oxygen level is dropping?
explanation: You got it! The brain is super sensitive to oxygen. When it starts running low, the patient often gets fidgety, anxious, or confused before anything else happens. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h7)

question: Which sign tells you a patient is struggling and working extra hard to breathe?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles in the neck during inhalation
options.B: Warm and dry skin across the chest and arms
options.C: A slow and steady heart rate below 60 beats per minute
options.D: Quiet and effortless breathing sounds throughout both lung fields

explanation: Correct! When normal breathing isn't enough, the body recruits extra muscles in the neck and shoulders to help pull air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why do we teach pursed-lip breathing to patients with chronic lung issues?

options.A: It lowers the patient's blood pressure immediately
options.B: It stops all coughing episodes within a few minutes
options.C: It replaces the need for using oxygen therapy
options.D: It keeps airways open longer and helps expel trapped air

explanation: Well done! Breathing out through pursed lips creates a gentle back-pressure, stopping tiny airways from collapsing too soon. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h8)

question: What is the best way to help prevent atelectasis in a patient after surgery?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the chest
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill to ensure total rest
options.C: Encouraging regular deep breathing and incentive spirometry
options.D: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed to rest the lungs

explanation: Spot on! Getting the patient to take deep breaths and use their incentive spirometer pops those little air sacs wide open and keeps the lungs clear. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h8)
